messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 19, Kofi had only recently started his first full-time job as a UX designer, proud of the small routines that made him feel adult: taking the same train into the city, wearing his badge at a startup office with glass meeting rooms, staying late to refine mockups before a product sprint. The stalking began in a way that, to him at first, felt too ambiguous to call anything. He noticed the same man more than once outside his apartment building and again near the coffee shop where he stopped before work. Then the sightings spread into the shape of his week. The man was across the street when Kofi left the office after dark, seated at the far end of a train car, standing near the entrance of the grocery store he used on Sundays. What made it frightening was not only recognition but the accumulating certainty of it. Kofi would look up and feel the jolt of seeing that familiar face already watching him, as if parts of his day were no longer his own.

Over time he began to move through ordinary spaces with the sense that anything could happen without warning. On evenings when he stayed late at the office to finish interface revisions, he found himself checking the reflections in the lobby glass before stepping outside. If someone paused too long near the entrance or seemed to be on the same block for more than a minute, his whole body tightened. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, not in an abstract way but in the practical geography of sidewalks, train platforms, apartment hallways, and office doors. The places that had once felt predictable now seemed full of openings through which danger could enter.

What stayed with him most from that period was the feeling of being studied. He remembered trying to convince himself he was overreacting, then seeing the man again in a setting that should have had nothing to do with the earlier encounters and feeling his stomach drop. In his mind, that repetition meant something: nowhere was protected simply because it should have been. Since then, Kofi had become certain that he had to stay especially alert because you never know what can happen next. He described scanning before unlocking his apartment door, checking behind him on the walk from the station, and choosing seats in public places where he could watch entrances. At work, during design reviews, part of his attention drifted toward the corridor outside the conference room whenever footsteps slowed near the glass. Even while discussing fonts or user flows, he was tracking movement, exits, and the possibility of being followed again.

Alongside that vigilance was a steady current of self-blame that he found hard to put down. He had come to believe the stalking had happened because of the way he acted. He replayed his own behavior repeatedly, wondering whether he had been too visible, too predictable, too polite, too unaware. If he had changed his route earlier, if he had not kept such regular hours, if he had noticed sooner what was happening, maybe none of it would have continued. He did not present these thoughts as guesses; he carried them like conclusions. When friends told him it was not his fault, he nodded without conviction. To him, their reassurance missed the point that his choices had made him easy to track.

In the months that followed, that logic narrowed his life. He varied his commute compulsively and sometimes left work early or lingered long after others had gone so he would not be outside at the “wrong” time. He stopped going to the same café near the office because being a regular there now felt reckless. At home he became cautious about routines, delaying errands or taking longer routes for no reason other than the fear of being predictable. The cost of this was visible. He was often tired at work after spending so much energy monitoring his surroundings, and his concentration slipped during tasks that once absorbed him. Colleagues noticed he was quieter and less spontaneous. He was single, and where he had once imagined city life opening outward for him, his days now felt organized around not being caught off guard.

By the time he sought help, Kofi was exhausted by the effort of trying to stay one step ahead of a threat that, in his mind, had proved itself capable of appearing anywhere. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic incident but the recognition that he no longer moved through his own life with any sense of ease. Even on uneventful days, he was braced. He wanted help because he was tired of feeling that every street and doorway required calculation, but what frightened him most was the idea of letting his guard down and being wrong. At the same time, he still hoped it might be possible to work, commute, and live like other people his age without feeling that danger was waiting just outside the frame.
